title: Projects
text:
Biophysical Settings describe the vegetation a place would have supported before Euro-American settlement, given the land and its historical disturbance regime. This summary covers Monongahela National Forest. The table is one row per setting.





Ten largest Biophysical Settings on Monongahela National Forest.




Central and Southern Appalachian Spruce-Fir Forest covers the most ground in this summary, about 454,640 acres. Oak forests and Appalachian (hemlock)–northern hardwood forest follow. Riparian systems and rocky oak-pine woodland are on the forest too, on much less area.

title: Projects
text:
Wooden Man Weather
Wooden Man Weather is a dashboard for Marquette and the central Upper Peninsula. It is built to be checked: the forecast beside the recent year, and how that year compares with normal. Same publishing tool as this site, different pace.

title: About
text:
I work with The Nature Conservancy’s LANDFIRE team. The assessments I publish are a way into a landscape: historical ecosystems, current vegetation, and the patterns a manager can actually use.
Two examples are on this site. The projects page charts Biophysical Settings for Monongahela National Forest. Wooden Man Weather is a smaller site, a weather dashboard for Marquette, Michigan.
The longer record — roles, collaborators, and the rest of the work — is on LinkedIn.
The painting on the home page is by Leo Barch. It was made for the Monongahela assessment.

title: Landscape assessments
text:
I am an ecologist with The Nature Conservancy’s LANDFIRE team. I publish landscape assessments so a forest’s history is something you can look at: which ecosystems covered the ground, and how much.
This site collects a few of those pieces. The Monongahela chart is a Biophysical Settings summary. Wooden Man Weather is a dashboard for Marquette, Michigan. A longer professional record is on LinkedIn.

The painting is assets/pixel_painting.png. The chart reads inputs/bps_monongahela.csv. The About page slideshow reads the files in assets/slides/. Shared settings — the site title, navbar, theme, and footer — live in _quarto.yml. The pages run full width: page-layout: full in that file, and the column grid in styles.css.

title: Instructions
text:
YAML
Each .qmd file opens with a block between --- lines. That block belongs to one page. Home looks like this:
---
title: "Landscape assessments"
subtitle: "Charts and short sites from ecological data"
---
_quarto.yml belongs to the whole site. The navbar is why Home, Projects, and About sit on the left, and why Instructions and LinkedIn sit on the right:
website:
  title: "Randy Swaty"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: projects.qmd
        text: Projects
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About
    right:
      - href: instructions.qmd
        text: Instructions
      - icon: linkedin
        href: https://www.linkedin.com/in/randyswaty/
project: type: website tells Quarto to publish these pages together and write the HTML to docs/. format: html chooses the Flatly theme and styles.css.

title: Instructions
Instructions
text:
Make it your portfolio

Change the site title in _quarto.yml, and the titles in index.qmd and about.qmd.
Swap assets/pixel_painting.png for your own image, and rewrite the caption on the home page.
Replace the files in assets/slides/ and the path list in the about-slides chunk on about.qmd. That chunk is a slickR slideshow.
Put your table in inputs/, point read.csv() at it, and rewrite the paragraphs on projects.qmd so they describe your result.
Replace the Wooden Man Weather link, in the footer and on the home and projects pages, with a project of yours. The other off-site link on this demo is LinkedIn.
To add a page, create a new .qmd file and add a matching href under navbar in _quarto.yml.

Keep the portfolio pages in the voice of the work. Put notes to yourself, folder maps, and render steps on a page like this one.
